sections.heading: Overview
sections.content:
The Unilateral Leg Extension is a single-leg isolation exercise performed on a plate-loaded leg extension machine.

By working one leg at a time, this variation addresses strength imbalances, increases quad activation, and allows greater focus on the target muscle.

This is a valuable accessory movement for quad development and can help reveal and fix left-right weaknesses.

sections.heading: Benefits
sections.content:
- Identifies and corrects left-right leg imbalances
- Focused quadriceps isolation
- Improved mind-muscle connection
- Reduced compensatory patterns
- Great for rehab and return-to-training work
- Allows each leg to be trained to true failure
- Lower back and hip-flexor friendly compared to bilateral version

sections.heading: Muscles Worked
sections.content:
Primary: Quadriceps (Rectus Femoris, Vastus Lateralis, Vastus Medialis, Vastus Intermedius)

Secondary: Hip Flexors, Stabilizing Core Muscles

sections.heading: Starting Position
sections.content:
1. Adjust the seat and footpad of the leg extension machine to your desired settings.
2. Load an appropriate weight plate onto the machine.
3. Sit on the machine with your back against the backrest.
4. Position your feet securely under the footpad.
5. Ensure your knees are aligned with the machine's pivot point.
6. Grip the handles or the seat edge for stability.
7. Keep the non-working leg relaxed.

sections.heading: Execution
sections.content:
1. Extend one leg fully, pushing against the footpad.
2. Keep your back against the backrest throughout.
3. Exhale as you perform the extension.
4. Squeeze the quad at the top of the movement.
5. Keep your movement controlled and avoid using momentum.
6. Inhale as you slowly lower the weight by bending your knee.
7. Return to the starting position under control.
8. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions on one leg before switching to the other.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- Lifting the back off the pad
- Using momentum to swing the weight up
- Incomplete range of motion at the top
- Dropping the weight on the return
- Not aligning the knee with the pivot point
- Tensing the non-working leg or upper body
- Turning the foot in/out (unless intentional)
- Using too much weight and losing form

sections.heading: Equipment Needed
sections.content:
- Plate-Loaded Leg Extension Machine
- Weight Plates
- Optional: Knee Sleeves
- Flat-soled shoes recommended
- Comfortable training attire
- Water bottle

sections.heading: Body Setup
sections.content:
1. Seat: Back flush against the backrest.
2. Knees: Aligned with the machine's pivot point.
3. Foot Position: Ankle just under the footpad.
4. Non-Working Leg: Relaxed and out of the way.
5. Hips: Seated fully into the seat.
6. Back: Flat against the pad throughout.
7. Hands: Gripping the handles or seat edges.
8. Core: Lightly braced for stability.

sections.heading: Progression Tips
sections.content:
1. Start with light weight to learn the pattern.
2. Begin with the weaker leg and match reps on the stronger side.
3. Pause at the top for 1-2 seconds for peak contraction.
4. Control the lowering phase to increase time under tension.
5. Gradually increase weight as strength improves.
6. Use sets of 10-15 reps for hypertrophy.
7. Add a 1 and 1/4 rep technique for extra intensity.
8. Avoid full lockout under heavy load if you have knee issues.

Bulgarian Split Squat: Unilateral compound
Single Leg Press: Machine-based unilateral
Step Up: Functional unilateral work
Goblet Squat: Quad-friendly compound
Sissy Squat: Bodyweight quad isolation

sections.heading: If You Have Limitations
sections.content:
Knee Pain: Reduce range of motion and avoid full lockout
Imbalance Issues: Start with the weaker side and match volume
Hip Flexor Tightness: Warm up thoroughly before starting
Limited Mobility: Shorten the range of motion
No Unilateral Machine: Use a standard leg extension one leg at a time
Beginner: Start light and focus on smooth, controlled reps
